reason: Croatia matches Moldova on the requirement, issuing and accepting the card at accession, and is the only case in which the card was issued. It does not match on the problem: a search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found none showing a missing national card or health information system, and by 2013 HZZO issued national health insurance cards and ran the infrastructure for using CEZIH, while the Commission had found Croatia advanced in e-health in 2012. Moldova's gap is the absence of both, rooted in weak administrative capacity and insufficient resources, and the Croatian evidence dates from 2011 to 2014.

Montenegro matches on the issue and the capacity mechanism: the Commission asks it to adapt its health information system for the card, equip its health insurance fund and budget for reimbursements by accession, against Moldova's requirement for IT infrastructure, systems and capacity for the EHIC scheme, and both countries have a feasibility study and adopted an action plan in 2026. The context differs: Montenegro already has an integrated health information system and recognises the card in law, while Moldova has no such system and has not transposed the EU acts on the card, and Montenegro has provisionally closed Chapter 2.

Serbia's 2025 key recommendation on IT infrastructure for the card is worded almost as Moldova's, and the Commission recorded no developments on the card in 2024, 2025 and 2026, as it recorded no progress for Moldova in 2025, but that is a match on the EU's request and on a stall, not on the problem. A search of all 90 Serbian evidence passages in the project found none on a national health insurance card, a health information system or a Serbian measure for the card, so whether Serbia faces Moldova's missing preconditions is unknown. Since Moldova finalised a feasibility study and approved an action plan in August 2026, the stall no longer matches its position either, and the case shows no route to closing the gap.

Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: a secondary act fixing the card's validity, form and issuing, with the health insurer as the issuing body, could work in Moldova, where CNAM already coordinates the card and a draft order on its technical specifications exists. This is conditional on Moldova first building what Croatia had in place by 2013, a national health insurance card and a central health information system, which the Croatian case does not show how to do.

Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: the route of a feasibility study, an action plan and legal recognition of the card, followed by adapting the health information system, equipping the insurer and budgeting for reimbursements, fits Moldova, which has already taken the first two steps. This is conditional on Moldova having an integrated health information system to adapt, which Montenegro already had, and on the EU accepting any deferral of the card to accession, which the evidence does not show.

Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: the Serbian evidence contains no measure or mechanism that could be applied in Moldova, only three years of unchanged Commission wording with no stated reason. It serves as a contrast, but there is no lesson whose transfer can be rated.

The Commission reported preparations continuing in 2011 and reaching completion in 2012, and HZZO reports that in 2013 one of its services issued the card and its Rijeka and Split offices processed or issued thousands of cards and certificates. HZZO also states that EU insured persons used the card in Croatia after accession. All evidence after accession is HZZO's own reporting, partly machine translated, with regional figures only and no independent confirmation.

The Commission states that the regulation was adopted in December 2011 and sets the card's validity, form and issuing details. A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found none naming the regulation after December 2011, and the 2013 issuing figures do not name it, so the card was issued in 2013 but its issue under this regulation is not shown.

In 2012 hardware for CEZIH was procured and a migration carried out, due for completion by May 2013, and in 2013 an HZZO service managed the public key infrastructure described as the basis for using CEZIH. A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found none giving usage data or confirming that the migration or the upgrade planned for 2013 was completed, so in_practice is not supported.

HZZO's central information system was in place in 2012, when its hardware was migrated together with CEZIH's, with completion due by May 2013, and a further upgrade was planned for 2013. A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found none confirming the migration or the upgrade, or giving usage data.

A tender for consolidating all registers in the health system was launched in 2012. A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found none stating the award, the work or its completion.

HZZO reports that in 2013 it agreed with the foreign and defence ministries a procedure for issuing the card to their officials. Whether this was before or after accession is not stated, and a search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found none showing cards issued under it.

The Commission states in 2024, 2025 and 2026 that the Law on compulsory health insurance recognises the card but that the card will be introduced only after accession. The adoption date of the provision is not stated, and the card cannot yet have been introduced.

The 2025 key recommendation asked for the study by the end of 2025, and the Commission reports in 2026 that it was updated with 2025 statistical data and that its findings were integrated into the action plan. The dates of the study and of its update are not stated.

The Government adopted the plan in February 2026, and the plan outlines the technical and IT upgrades for the card required before accession. A search of all 204 Montenegrin evidence passages in the project for the card, the health information system and the Health Insurance Fund found none reporting any of those upgrades carried out.

The Commission's 2026 key recommendation describes the Integrated Health Information System as existing and asks for it to be improved and adapted for issuing and applying the card by accession. It gives no description of the system or its use, and a search of all 204 Montenegrin evidence passages in the project found none reporting the adaptation started, so this status rests on the Commission's description of the system as existing and covers the system as it stands, not its use for the card.

The only statement of the outcome comes from HZZO, the body that issues and accepts the card, and gives no figure ('a vast number'). A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found no independent source on the card after accession, so success cannot be judged on the issuer's reporting alone.

HZZO names the card as the means by which EU insured persons received care in Croatia, but this is the issuer's own unquantified statement, with no comparison, and a search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project found no independent source recording the outcome. There is therefore nothing independent to which the card's contribution could be attributed.
